name: Tim Hecker
label: Kranky
lede: Tim Hecker was a policy analyst for the Canadian government before he left to study noise at McGill. He has put pipe organs through distortion, a falling piano on a record cover, and spent twenty years arguing that ambient music shouldn't be background.

eras.title: A techno alias and a civil-service desk
eras.text: Born in Vancouver in 1974 to two art teachers, Tim Hecker played in high-school rock bands before a sampler pulled him toward electronics. He made techno as Jetone, moved to Montreal, and started releasing drifting, crackling records under his own name while working for the Canadian government.

years.h: Tim Hecker starts out making techno as Jetone
years.p: The first releases come out under the alias Jetone, on labels in the orbit of German experimental techno such as Mille Plateaux and Force Inc.

years.h: Hecker trades Vancouver for Montreal and Concordia
years.p: He moves to study at Concordia University. Montreal stays his base for the next two decades.

years.h: Fed up with Jetone, Hecker puts out Haunt Me, Haunt Me Do It Again
years.p: His debut under his own name comes out on Montreal's Alien8 Recordings.
years.xp: By day Hecker was a policy analyst for the Canadian government. The records were a side job to a civil-service career, and he kept the desk job until 2006.

years.cap: Tim Hecker live at MassArt, Boston
years.h: Radio Amor starts with a Honduran shrimp fisherman named Jimmy
years.p: Recorded in Montreal and Halifax in 2001–02 and released on Mille Plateaux, it grew from Hecker's 1990s trip to Honduras, where he met Jimmy.
years.xp:
Hecker said he was totally obsessed with the idea of fishermen in the Caribbean. Pitchfork's Mark Richardson called Radio Amor his coldest and most piercing work.

Alien8 reissued it in 2007 and Kranky did again in 2018.

years.h: Mirages is the heavy one
years.p: Hecker's third album, on Alien8. He later described Harmony in Ultraviolet as keeping the heaviness of Mirages while adding melody.

eras.title: Out of the government, into organ and static
eras.text: In 2006 Tim Hecker left his government job, enrolled in a PhD at McGill and joined the Chicago drone label Kranky. His first album there, built from pipe organ and guitar run through distortion, is still the one critics reach for.

years.h: Hecker leaves the civil service for a PhD at McGill
years.p: His thesis on urban noise, published in 2014 as The era of megaphonics: on the productivity of loud sound, 1880–1930, led to a lectureship in sound culture at McGill.

years.cap: Tim Hecker with Isis, improvised set, Bleeding Edge Festival, Saratoga, August 13, 2006
years.h: Harmony in Ultraviolet puts a pipe organ through distortion
years.p: Hecker's first album for Kranky, recorded in Montreal and Banff, also runs guitars and strings through the fuzz. Pitchfork later ranked it the ninth best ambient album of all time.
years.xp:
The title riffs on Henri Matisse's painting Harmony in Red, with ultraviolet picked because it can't be seen. Hecker shot the cover himself: the Monument to Fallen Partisans in Bologna's Piazza Maggiore, a memorial to the Italian Resistance, chosen for its crude qualities.

Tracks like Radio Spiricom, named for a 1980s device that claimed to talk to the dead, and the 13-minute Whitecaps of White Noise suite made the record loud and dense for an ambient album. Pitchfork gave it 8.7 and made it the 14th best album of 2006.

years.cap: Tim Hecker at Musikzimmer, Aarau, May 28, 2009
years.h: Hecker's second Kranky record is An Imaginary Country
years.p: It comes out around the time he tours with [[Godspeed You! Black Emperor|3648db01-b29d-4ab9-835c-83f6a5068fe4]] and [[Sigur Rós|f6f2326f-6b25-4170-b89d-e235b25508e8]].

eras.title: One day in a Reykjavík church
eras.text: With Ben Frost as engineer and co-conspirator, Tim Hecker recorded a pipe organ in an Icelandic church in a single day and spent months tearing it apart. Ravedeath, 1972 won a Juno, and Virgins became his best-reviewed record.

years.cap: Tim Hecker at Cafe OTO, London, May 19, 2010
years.h: Ben Frost finds the church; Hecker gets one day with its organ
years.p: At Fríkirkjan in Reykjavík, Hecker tracks the pipe organ plus guitar and piano in a single day, then takes the tapes home to Montreal and Banff to rebuild them.

years.big: "The wrongest and the most right title ever."
yt: Virginal I / The Piano Drop, Pitchfork Festival 2012
years.h: A piano goes off a roof, and the record wins a Juno
years.p: Hecker on the name of Ravedeath, 1972 (Kranky, krank154). The cover is a 1972 photo of MIT students pushing a piano off Baker House; the album takes the Juno for Electronic Album of the Year.
years.xp:
Hecker licensed the photo from MIT's archives and re-photographed it, inspired by images of mass media being destroyed, like pirated DVDs crushed by bulldozers. The track titles keep the theme going: The Piano Drop, Hatred of Music, Studio Suicide, 1980.

Metacritic scored it 86. It was longlisted for the Polaris Prize, placed third on The Quietus's 2011 list, and later landed at No. 136 on Pitchfork's 200 best albums of the 2010s.

years.cap: Tim Hecker at Pitchfork Music Festival, Chicago, July 13, 2012
years.h: Daniel Lopatin proposes a team-up, and Instrumental Tourist follows
years.p: Lopatin, who records as Oneohtrix Point Never, gets days of improvising at Mexican Summer's studio, edited down Teo Macero style and released on his Software label.
years.xp: The two had admired each other's work without ever meeting formally. Hecker said the album took shape almost unconsciously, through joking around.

years.h: Hecker's Milan Cathedral cover for Virgins echoes Abu Ghraib
years.p: The cover shows a statue of the Virgin Mary covered for restoration. Recorded in Reykjavík, Seattle and Troy, New York, with woodwinds, piano and synths.
years.xp: Hecker described the record's rhythmic, staccato, aggressive blasts as deliberately hostile to the ambient label. With [[Kara-Lis Coverdale|aabe385c-379a-467f-9a6d-2560ffa0b730]], [[Valgeir Sigurðsson|b47171a4-1bfc-4d80-a91e-33c368fa6a5a]] and Ben Frost playing, it scored 87 on Metacritic, his best ever, placed fifth in The Wire's critics' poll and was longlisted for the 2014 Polaris Prize.

eras.title: 4AD, a choir, and gagaku players in a Tokyo temple
eras.text: Tim Hecker finished his doctorate, signed to 4AD, worked with a choir scored by Jóhann Jóhannsson, then went back to Kranky for two records made with a Japanese gagaku ensemble. Film directors started calling.

years.cap: Tim Hecker live at Korzo, The Hague, during Rewire, May 13, 2016
years.h: Signed to 4AD, Hecker books an Icelandic choir for Love Streams
years.p: Recorded in Reykjavík with the Icelandic Choir Ensemble, vocals arranged by Jóhann Jóhannsson. Hecker's stated themes: liturgical aesthetics after Yeezus, and the voice in the age of auto-tune.

years.h: Hecker scores his first feature, The Free World
years.p: Jason Lew's drama is selected for the 2016 Sundance U.S. Dramatic Competition.

years.h: Hecker takes Konoyo to a temple outside Tokyo
years.p: Back on Kranky, he builds the album from sessions with the Tokyo Gakuso ensemble at Jiunzan Mandala-Temple Kanzouin, with shō, hichiriki and ryuteki woodwinds.
years.xp: Cellist Mariel Roberts and Kara-Lis Coverdale also play, with Ben Frost engineering. Metacritic scored it 81, and it reached No. 18 on the UK Dance Albums chart.

yt: Full set with the Konoyo Ensemble, Primavera Sound, June 1, 2019
years.h: Anoyo answers Konoyo with the other world
years.p: Konoyo means this world; Anoyo means the other. The second record from the sessions completes Hecker's pair of gagaku albums.

eras.title: Against the wellness playlist
eras.text: Through the pandemic Tim Hecker took up Buddhism and meditated in his studio, scored a BBC drama and a Brandon Cronenberg horror film, and made an album aimed squarely at the soothing ambient filling streaming playlists.

years.h: A former Catholic, Hecker takes up Buddhism
years.p: During the COVID-19 pandemic he starts studying it and practicing meditation in his studio.

years.h: Hecker scores The North Water and Luzifer in the same year
years.p: Andrew Haigh's BBC Arctic whaling drama, and Peter Brunner's Austrian film, which won Franz Rogowski best actor at Fantastic Fest.

years.h: Infinity Pool premieres at Sundance with a Hecker score
years.p: Brandon Cronenberg's sci-fi horror stars Alexander Skarsgård and Mia Goth.

years.h: No Highs takes aim at corporate ambient
years.p: Kranky's press release pitches it as a beacon of unease against false positive corporate ambient. [[Colin Stetson|22b2f6dc-fcc2-490d-a462-f972a692ce12]] plays saxophone on Total Garbage and Monotony II.

years.h: Shards, a new EP
years.p: Hecker's latest release.
